requirements.text: Energy. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:

children.text: Create a list of 15 items of your personal "stuff." Classify each item as an essential need (such as soap) or a desirable want (such as a video game). Identify any excess "stuff" you no longer need, working with your family, if possible. Donate, repurpose, or recycle those items you can.

List five ways having too much "stuff" affects you, your family, your community, AND the world. For each of the five ways, consider the following aspects: the financial impact, time spent, maintenance, health, storage, and waste generation. Identify practices that can be used to avoid accumulating too much "stuff."

notes: Resources: Pacific Garbage Patch (video)
Know Your Plastics (video)
Recycling E-Waste (video)
children.text: Research the impact waste has on the environment (land, water, air). Find out what the trash vortex is and how it was formed. Explain the number system for plastic recyclables and which plastics are more commonly recycled. Identify the average lifespan of one electronic device in your household, and whether it can be recycled in whole or part.

notes: Resources:Decluttering (video)
Why Do We Have So Much Stuff? (video)
requirements.text: Stuff. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:

notes: Resources: Sustainable Development Goals (video)
Sustainable Goals (video)
Clean Water Goal (video)
children.text: The United Nations lists 17 Sustainable Development Goals. These include Zero Hunger, Clean Water and Sanitation, Affordable and Clean Energy, Sustainable Cities and Community, Responsible Consumption and Production, Climate Action, Life Below Water, and Life on Land. Pick one of these eight and summarize the goal and its current and future impact on you, your family, community, and the world.

notes: Resources:Planetary Cycles (video)
Earth's Systems (video)
4 Spheres of Earth (video)
children.text: Identify how the planetary life-support systems (soil, climate, freshwater, atmospheric, nutrient, oceanic, ecosystems, and species) support life on Earth and interact with one another. Share what happens to the planet's sustainability when these systems are disrupted by natural events or human activity.

notes: Resources:Product Life Cycle Assessment (video)
Life Cycle Assessment Principles (video)
Product Life Cycles (video)
children.text: Identify how product life cycles (the cycle of design, sourcing, production, use, and disposal or reuse) influence current and future sustainability. Choose one common product to demonstrate how the full product life cycle would apply.

notes: Resources: Population Affects Resources (video)
How Population Growth Impacts the Planet (video)
children.text: Learn how the world's population affects the sustainability of Earth. Discuss three human activities that may contribute to putting Earth at risk, now and in the future.

notes: Resources:Should We Let Pandas Go Extinct? (video)
Extinction Explained (video)
Stop Extinction! (video)
children.text: Explain the term species (plant or animal) decline. Share the human activities that contribute to species decline, what can be done to help reverse the decline, and its impact on a sustainable environment.

notes: Resources:Global Warming From 1880 to 2022 (video)
Global Temps Since 1850 (video)
Timelapse of Planet Changes (video)
children.text: Find a world map that shows the pattern of temperature change for a period of at least 100 years. Identify three factors that scientists believe affect the global weather and temperature. Discuss how climate change impacts sustainability of food, water, or other resources.

requirements.text: Do TWO of the following and discuss with your counselor:

notes: Resources:Sustainable Camping Tips (Packing & Hiking) (video)
What Does LNT Means to Scouts (video)
children.text: On a campout or other outdoor Scouting activity that you attend, make notes on the sustainability practices you and your fellow Scouts practice. Observe transportation, forestry, soil conservation, water resources, habitat, buildings, campsites, and sanitation. Share what you observed and learned with your counselor.

notes: Resources: Camping Tricks: The Scout Turn Around Rule LNT (video)
Leave No Trace—And There's a Song! (video)
children.text: Discuss with your counselor how living by the Scout Oath, Scout Law, Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code in your daily life helps promote sustainability.

notes: Resources:Sustainability in Your Life (video)
10 Ways to Take Care of the Environment (video)
children.text: Identify 5 behavioral changes that you and your family can make to improve the sustainability of your household. Share and discuss each with your counselor.

requirements.text: Do the following:

notes: Resources:Career Paths in Sustainability (video)
Green Jobs- Building for the Future (video)
Sustainability Careers (video)
requirements.text: Learn about career opportunities in the sustainability field. Pick one and find out the education, training, and experience required. Discuss what you have learned with your counselor and explain why this career might interest you.

swimming.name: Swimming
swimming.overview: Merit Badge Pamphlets are now free and publicly available. Note: Always check www.scouting.org/skills/merit-badges/all/ for the latest requirements.

notes: Resources: Safe Swim Defense (website)
Rip Current Survival Guide (website w/ video)
Safe Swimming Area (website)
children.text: Review with your counselor how Scouting America's Safe Swim Defense guidelines anticipates and deals with common drowning situations such as unfenced residential pools, nonswimmers entering deep water, risky behaviors, medical impairment in the water, drop-offs, cold water, murky water, river currents, rip currents, and surf.

notes: Resource: 10 Common Summer Safety Emergencies (website)
children.text: Discuss the prevention and treatment of health concerns that could occur while swimming, including hypothermia, dehydration, sunburn, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, muscle cramps, hyperventilation, spinal injury, stings and bites, and cuts and scrapes.

requirements.text: Do the following:

notes: Resource: Swimming Merit Badge Pamphlet (PDF)
requirements.text: Before doing the following requirements, successfully complete the Scouting America swimmer test, found in the Swimming merit badge pamphlet.

notes: Resources: Learn To Swim Freestyle | A Simple Step-by-Step Guide (video)
How To Swim Front Crawl? (video)
children.text: Demonstrate the front crawl or the trudgen using good form.

notes: Resources: How To Swim Backstroke (video)
How To Swim Backstroke (video)
children.text: Demonstrate the back crawl using good form.

notes: Resource: How To Swim Side Stroke (video)
children.text: Demonstrate the sidestroke using good form.

notes: Resources: How To Swim Breaststroke Properly! (video)
How To Swim Breaststroke (video)
The Elements of Breaststroke (video)
children.text: Demonstrate the breaststroke using good form.

notes: Resource: Learn To Swim Elementary Backstroke (video)
children.text: Demonstrate the elementary backstroke using good form.

requirements.text: Correctly perform the following strokes:

Swim continuously for 150 yards in a strong manner using each of the following strokes in any order; front crawl or trudgen (25 yards); back crawl (25 yards); sidestroke (25 yards); breaststroke (25 yards); and elementary backstroke (50 yards).

children.text: Demonstrate water rescue methods by reaching with your arm or leg, by reaching with a suitable object, and by throwing lines and objects. Explain why swimming rescues should not be attempted when a reaching or throwing rescue is possible, and explain why and how a rescue swimmer should avoid contact with the victim.
With a helper and a practice victim, show a line rescue both as tender and as rescuer. The practice victim should be approximately 30 feet from shore in deep water.

requirements.text: Do the following:

notes: Resource: How To Float on Your Back for Beginners | Watch This Before You Give Up (video)
children.text: Float faceup in a resting position for at least three minutes with minimal movement.
Demonstrate survival floating for at least five minutes.

notes: Resource: PFD's H.E.L.P. & Huddle Positions (video)
children.text: While wearing a properly fitted U.S. Coast Guard-approved life jacket, demonstrate the HELP and huddle positions. Explain their purposes.
Explain why swimming or survival floating will hasten the onset of hypothermia in cold water.

requirements.text: Do the following:

notes: Resource: How To Do a Feetfirst Surface Dive (video)
children.text: Use the feetfirst method of surface diving and bring an object up from the bottom.

notes: Resource: How To Do a Headfirst Surface Dive (video)
children.text: Do a headfirst surface dive (pike or tuck), and bring the object up again.
Do a headfirst surface dive to a depth of at least 5 feet and swim underwater for three strokes. Come to the surface, take a breath, and repeat the sequence twice.

requirements.text: In water over your head, but not to exceed 10 feet, do the following:

notes: Note: If your state, city, or local community requires a water depth greater than 7 feet, it is important to abide by that mandate.
requirements.text: Following the guidelines set in the Scouting America Safe Swim Defense guidelines, in water at least 7 feet deep, show a standing headfirst dive from a dock or pool deck. Show a long shallow dive, also from the dock or pool deck.

notes: Resources: What Happens to Your Body When You Swim? (video)
10 Health Benefits of Swimming (video)
requirements.text: Explain the health benefits of regular aerobic exercise, and discuss why swimming is favored as both fitness and therapeutic exercise.

textile.name: Textile
textile.overview: Merit Badge Pamphlets are now free and publicly available. Note: Always check www.scouting.org/skills/merit-badges/all/ for the latest requirements.

notes: Resource: Textiles: What Are They? Where Do They Come From? (video)
requirements.text: Discuss with your counselor the importance of textiles. Explain the terms fiber, fabric, and textile. Give examples of textiles you use every day.

children.text: Get swatches of two natural fiber fabrics (100 percent cotton, linen, wool or silk; no blends). Get swatches of two synthetic fiber fabrics (nylon, polyester, acrylic, olefin, or spandex). Get a sample of one cellulosic fabric (rayon, acetate or lyocell).

notes: Resource: Natural vs Synthetic Fibers (Which to Choose and Why) (video)
children.text: Give the origin, major characteristics, and general content of each type of fiber obtained for 2(a). Explain the difference between a cellulosic manufactured fiber and a synthetic manufactured fiber.

notes: Resources: From Cotton to Yarn (video)
Weaving Process (video)
Knitting Process (video)
Complete Process of Textile Manufacturing Fiber to Complete Garments (video)
children.text: Describe the main steps in making raw fiber into yarn, and yarn into fabric.
Assume you will soon buy a new garment or other textile item. Tell your counselor what fiber or blend of fibers you want the item to be, and give reasons for your choice.

requirements.text: Do the following:

children.text: Visit a textile plant, textile products manufacturer, or textile school or college. Report on what you saw and learned.

notes: Resource: How To Make a Cardboard Loom (website)
children.text: Weave a belt, headband, placemat, or wall hanging using a simple loom that you have made yourself.

notes: Resource: Woven vs. Knit vs. Non-Woven Fabrics | Textile Talk w/ A Thrifty Notion (video)
children.text: With a magnifying glass, examine a woven fabric, a nonwoven fabric, and a knitted fabric. Sketch what you see. Explain how the three constructions are different.

notes: Resource: Wet Felting Tutorial for Beginners (video)
children.text: Make a piece of felt.

notes: Resources: Natural Dyes From Plants and Vegetables | DIY Eco-Friendly Dyes | Homeschool with Everyday Food (video)
Short Tie Dye Demo - No Narration (video)
Short Tie Dye Demo - With Narration (video)
children.text: Make two natural dyes and use them to dye a garment or a piece of fabric.

notes: Resources: A Simple DIY Way to Waterproof Anything (video)
DIY Seam Seal (video)
children.text: Waterproof a fabric.

notes: Resource: Identification of Basic Textile Fibers by Polarized Light Microscopy (video)
children.text: Demonstrate how to identify fibers, using microscope identification or the breaking test.

requirements.text: Do TWO of the following:

notes: Resource: Loom and Weaving Terminology (video)
requirements.text: Explain the meaning of 10 of the following terms: warp, harness, heddle, shed, aramid, spandex, sliver, yarn, spindle, distaff, loom, cellulose, sericulture, extrusion, carbon fibers, spinneret, staple, worsted, nonwoven, and greige goods.

notes: Resource: The Ultimate Fabric Guide - The Differences Between Natural vs Synthetic vs Semi-Synthetic Fibers (video)
requirements.text: List the advantages and disadvantages of natural plant fibers, natural animal fibers, cellulosic manufactured fibers, and synthetic manufactured fibers. Identify and discuss at least four ecological concerns regarding the production and care of textiles.

notes: Resources: Day in the Life of a Textile Engineer (video)
Careers in the Fashion & Textiles Industry (video)
Textile Engineering Careers (video)
Want To Work in the Textiles Industry? (video)
requirements.text: Explain to your counselor, either verbally or in a written report, five career possibilities in the textile industry. Tell your counselor about two positions that interest you the most and the education, cost of training, and specific duties those positions require.

theater.name: Theater
theater.overview: Merit Badge Pamphlets are now free and publicly available. Note: Always check www.scouting.org/skills/merit-badges/all/ for the latest requirements.

notes: Note: Watching plays on television, video, or as a movie is not permitted.
Resource: Theatre Merit Badge (video)
requirements.text: See or read three full-length plays. Write a review of each. Discuss with your counselor the plot or story. If you chose to watch the plays, comment on the acting and the staging.

notes: Resource: How to Write a One-Act Play (video)
requirements.text: Write a one-act play that will take at least 10 minutes to perform. The play must have a main character, conflict, and a climax.

children.text: Act a major part in a full-length play; or act a part in three one-act plays.
Direct a play. Cast, rehearse, and stage it. The play must be at least 10 minutes long.
Design the set for a play or a theatrical production. Make a model of it.
Design the costumes for five characters in a theatrical production set in a historical time.
Show skill in hair and makeup design. Make up yourself or a friend as a historical figure, a clown, an extraterrestrial, or a monster as directed.
With your counselor's approval, help with the building and painting of the scenery for a theatrical production.
With your counselor's approval, design the lighting for a play; or help install, focus, color, program, and operate the lighting for a theatrical production.
With your counselor's approval, help install, focus, equalize, program, and operate the sound for a theatrical production.
Serve as the stage manager for a theatrical production. Document all cues and stage setups in your calling script.
Serve as musical director for a musical theater production.

notes: Resource: General Safety in the Theatre (video)
requirements.text: Discuss with your counselor the safety precautions that should be practiced when working in a theater to protect the cast and crew. Then do THREE of the following:

children.text: You have come into a large room. It is full of pictures, furniture, and other things of interest.
As you are getting on a bus, your books fall into a puddle. By the time you pick them up, the bus has driven off.
You have failed a school test. You are talking with your teacher, who does not buy your story.
You are at camp with a new Scout. You try to help them pass a cooking test. The Scout learns very slowly.
You are at a banquet. The meat is good. You don't like the vegetable. The dessert is ice cream.
You are a circus performer such as a juggler, high-wire artist, or lion tamer doing a routine.

notes: Resource: What is Pantomime? (video)
requirements.text: Mime or pantomime any ONE of the following, chosen by your counselor.

notes: Resource: Stage Anatomy (video)
requirements.text: Explain the following: proscenium arch, central or arena staging, center stage, stage right, stage left, downstage, upstage, stage crew, flies, portal, cyclorama, stage brace, spotlight, floodlight, lighting control board, sound mixing desk, thrust staging, ground plans, and sightlines.

traffic-safety.name: Traffic Safety
traffic-safety.overview: Merit Badge Pamphlets are now free and publicly available. Note: Always check www.scouting.org/skills/merit-badges/all/ for the latest requirements.

notes: Resource: Distracted Driving (video)
children.text: Explain why a distracted driver must not operate a motor vehicle. List five common distractions, explain how driver distractions contribute to traffic accidents, and tell how drivers can minimize distractions.

notes: Resources: The Deadly Truth About Drinking and Driving (video)
Blood Alcohol Content & Driving: What You Need to Know (video)
children.text: Explain why a driver impaired by alcohol, drugs, or other substances must not operate a motor vehicle. Describe how alcohol, cold medications, and prescription and illegal drugs affect driving abilities. For the state where you live, find out what is the legal blood alcohol concentration and what are the consequences for driving while intoxicated or driving under the influence. Find out what the open-container law is in your state.

notes: Resources: Recognizing Fatigue—Warning Signs (video)
Driver Tiredness, Fatigue, and Road Safety (video)
children.text: Explain why a fatigued driver must not operate a motor vehicle. Describe how drivers must plan to be alert for safely transporting families, friends, Scouts, and themselves.

notes: Resources: 7 Common Mistakes New Drivers Make—and How to Avoid Them (website)
Most Common Driving Mistakes to Avoid (video)
children.text: Describe mistakes that new drivers make, how those mistakes increase their risk of collisions, how drivers can reduce this risk, and how driving behavior affects automobile insurance rates.

requirements.text: Preventing Impaired Driving. Do the following:

notes: Resources: How to Wear a Seat Belt Properly (video)
Car Seat Safety (video)
children.text: Demonstrate how to wear a lap and shoulder belt properly. Explain why it is important for the driver and all passengers, including children sitting in age-appropriate seats, to always wear their seat belts.

notes: Resource: 10 Car Safety Features That Every Car Must Have (video)
children.text: List five safety features found in motor vehicles besides occupant restraint systems. Describe each safety feature, how each works, and how each contributes to safety.

requirements.text: Vehicle Safety. Do the following:

notes: Resource: Types of Car Lights & Their Purposes (video)
children.text: Demonstrate that all driving lights and signaling lights are clear and operational. Show where the switches are for these lights. Explain how drivers use lights to drive safely and courteously and to communicate with other drivers.

notes: Resource: How to Check Your Wipers (video)
children.text: Explain issues that might affect the driver's ability to see through the front, rear, and side windows. Demonstrate with a smear-and-clear test if the windshield wiper blades will clear the windshield completely or need to be replaced. Describe instances in good and bad weather when windshield wipers are important to safe driving.

notes: Resource: How to Check Your Tires (video)
children.text: Demonstrate how to find the vehicle's recommended tire pressures, how to check tire pressures, and how to check for adequate tire tread depth. Explain why proper tire pressure and tread depth are important to traction, stopping distances, tire wear, and fuel economy.

notes: Resource: Tire Inflator and Sealant Kit (video)
children.text: Check the vehicle for tools needed to change a flat tire or to use tire sealant to fix a puncture. Demonstrate you know how to change a flat tire and how to use tire sealant.

notes: Note: Use the graphics template in the Traffic Safety merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor to set up this demonstration.
Resources: Stopping Distance Table and Graphs (PDF)
Thinking, Braking, and Stopping Distances (video)
Stopping Distance Demonstration (video)
children.text: In a location away from traffic hazards, mark off the reaction distances and braking distances that a car will travel as it makes an emergency stop at 25, 55, and 70 miles per hour on level dry and level wet pavement. Discuss how these distances change for normal and impaired drivers, for day and night driving, and for weather conditions.

requirements.text: Auto Maintenance and Safety Checkups. With adult supervision and using a vehicle that you have access to, do the following:

notes: Resource: Bicycle Rules of the Road (video)
children.text: Describe at least three examples of traffic laws that apply to drivers of motor vehicles and to bicyclists.

notes: Resource: Traffic Stop Etiquette (video)
children.text: Explain procedures and etiquette a driver should follow if a law enforcement officer stops their vehicle.

notes: Resource: What to Do After a Car Accident (video)
children.text: Explain procedures that drivers should follow if they are involved in a car accident.

notes: Resource: Three Documents You Should Always Have in Your Car (website)
children.text: Name the three documents that drivers are required by law to carry whenever they operate a motor vehicle.

requirements.text: Traffic Safety and the Law. Do the following:

notes: Resource: How Highways Are Designed and Built (video)
children.text: Explain how road designs for intersections, medians, and road shoulders contribute to traffic safety. Discuss safety features of interstate highways.

notes: Resources: Understanding Road Signs (video)
Traffic Signals (video)
Pavement Markings (video)
children.text: Explain how color and shape help drivers recognize and understand the information presented on traffic and roadway signs. Explain the purpose of different types of signs, signals, and pavement markings.

requirements.text: Road Designs and Signs. Do the following:

notes: Resources: Bike Safety - Sharing the Road (video)
The Basics of Bicycle Safety (video)
What to Do to Make Driving at Night Safer (video)
children.text: Describe the difference in nighttime visibility between a properly lit bicycle and rider (or a pedestrian) wearing reflective material and a bicycle and rider with no lights (or a pedestrian) dressed in dark clothing without reflective material.

notes: Resource: The Basics of Pedestrian Safety (video)
children.text: Name at least four safety measures that pedestrians, including hikers, should follow as they walk along or across streets or roadways.

notes: Resource: Driving Safety 101: School Bus Safety (video)
children.text: Name at least four safety measures that drivers of motor vehicles should follow if they approach a school bus making its stops at pick-up and drop-off locations.

notes: Resources: Blind Spots Lessons (video)
Lane Changes (video)
children.text: Discuss the risks associated with blind spots on cars and trucks and how drivers can prevent lane change crashes.

requirements.text: Sharing the Road. Do the following:

notes: Resources: Engineering and Inspector Careers (video)
Women in Road Safety Careers (video)
children.text: Interview a traffic law enforcement officer or a traffic safety professional in your community to identify what three traffic safety problems the officer is most concerned about. Discuss with your counselor possible ways to solve one of those problems.

notes: Resources: Take the Pledge (website)
Parent-Teen Driving Agreement (website)
children.text: Write a personal traffic safety pledge, addressing three of your most concerning issues relating to traffic safety. Discuss your pledge with your counselor.

notes: Resource: Teen Driving Safety Event (video)
children.text: Initiate and organize an activity or event to demonstrate the importance of traffic safety.

requirements.text: Traffic, Your Community, and You. Do ONE of the following:

notes: Resources: What It's Like to Work in Traffic Control and Safety in Road Construction (video)
On The Job: Traffic Signal Technician (video)
requirements.text: Careers. Explore careers related to traffic safety. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Your research methods may include—with your parent or guardian's permission—an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career.

truck-transportation.name: Truck Transportation
truck-transportation.overview: Merit Badge Pamphlets are now free and publicly available. Note: Always check www.scouting.org/skills/merit-badges/all/ for the latest requirements.

notes: Resource: Search Trucking Companies - Find Carriers By City And State (website)
requirements.text: List the major truck lines serving your town.

notes: Resource: 10 Advantages of Road Transport (video)
children.text: Describe the role of truck transportation within commerce (the movement of goods, funds, and information).

notes: Resources: Transportation & Logistics Industry Overview - Introduction (video)
How Does Trucking Fit Into the Supply Chain? (video)
The Vital Role of Trucks in Transporting Goods: A Comprehensive Overview (website)
children.text: Describe how trucks fit into a company's supply chain. This could be a manufacturer, importer, wholesaler, or retailer.

notes: Resource: Global Supply Chain Management Explained: Key Players, Risks & Incoterms (video)
children.text: On paper, map out how goods that are manufactured overseas are transported to a retailer in this country.

requirements.text: Do the following:

notes: Resource: Diesel vs. Gasoline Engines: Key Differences Explained (video)
requirements.text: Describe the difference between the gasoline engine and the diesel engine that power trucks. List the advantages of each.

notes: Resources: How To Properly Maintain Fleets? (video)
How Trucking Companies Manage Fleet Maintenance Effectively | Part 1 (video)
How Trucking Companies Manage Fleet Maintenance Effectively | Part 2 (video)
children.text: Find out what kind of maintenance program the company follows to help keep its fleet, drivers, and the roadway safe.

notes: Resource: Communication with Dispatch (video)
children.text: Find out how dispatchers maintain communication with drivers on the road.

notes: Resources: Top 6 Safety Tips for Truck Drivers (video)
Essential Safety Tips, Every Female Trucker Needs to Stay Safe (video)
children.text: Talk with a professional truck driver about safety. Learn about the truck driver's rules of the road for safe driving. List five safe-driving rules every professional truck driver must follow.

notes: Resource: How to Fill Out a Logbook for CDL Drivers (website)
children.text: Review the driver's log and find out what kind of information the log contains.

notes: Resources: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) - Regulations Overview (website)
Federal Safety Regulations Limit a Long-Haul Truck Driver's Time on the Road (video)
Federal Regulations Every Truck Driver Should Know! (video)
children.text: Learn about important federal regulations that help ensure public safety.

requirements.text: Visit a truck terminal and complete items 4(a) through 4(e). After your visit, share what you have learned with your counselor.

children.text: Outline the general organization of a trucking company. Describe what each department does.

notes: Resource: 14 Jobs in the Trucking Industry Other Than Driving (website)
children.text: List five positions with trucking companies and describe each one.

requirements.text: Do the following:

notes: Resource: Trucking Industry (website)
requirements.text: Name five government agencies that work closely with the trucking industry. Describe their role.

notes: Resource: Different Types of Trucks and Their Uses (video)
requirements.text: List five different kinds of trucks. Tell the service each provides.

notes: Resources: How to Prepare Freight for Shipping to Avoid Damages (video)
How To Ship A Pallet: Preparing A Palletized LTL Freight Shipment Warehousing Tutorial (video)
How to Package Freight for Shipping (video)
children.text: How to prepare the shipment

notes: Resources: Mastering Load Board Bookings: A Step-by-Step Guide to Efficient Load Booking (video)
Truck Dispatcher and Broker Call Simulation - Negotiation Scenario #1 (video)
children.text: How to compare at least three carriers for time in transit and rates
How to choose which carrier to use

notes: Resource: Understanding Freight Shipping Insurance: A Comprehensive Guide (website)
children.text: How to insure the shipment for damages

requirements.text: Assume that you are going to ship by truck 500 pounds of goods (freight class 65) from your town to another town 500 miles away. Your shipment must arrive within three days. Explain in writing:

notes: Resources: Decoding Freight Abbreviations, Acronyms and Initialisms (video)
What's That? Bill of Lading (BOL) (video)
What's That? Intermodal & Multimodal (video)
What's That? Container vs. Trailer (video)
requirements.text: Explain the following terms: bill of lading, ETA, logbook, intermodal, containers, tariff, shippers, carrier, consignee, drayage, and cartage.

notes: Resources: What Career Opportunities are in Trucking? A LOT! (video)
What Life Is Like for a Trucker on the Road | NewsNation (video)
How to Become a Truck Dispatcher in 5 Steps? - Beginner Training (video)
Logistics Coordinator Job Description (video)
5 Must Have Skills to earn $10,000 a month as a Truck Dispatcher (video)
requirements.text: Explore careers related to this merit badge. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Your research methods may include—with your parent or guardian's permission—an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career.

veterinary-medicine.name: Veterinary Medicine

A Day in the Life of a Vet | If You See It, You Can Be It (video)

children.text: Poultry medicine

notes: Resources: A Career in Aquatic Animal Medicine (video)
How Does a Wildlife Veterinarian Do It?! (video)
children.text: Wildlife medicine and aquaculture medicine

children.text: Public health medicine and zoonotic disease surveillance and control

notes: Resource: Cool Jobs: Army Veterinarian (video)
children.text: The military

notes: Resource: Laboratory Animal Veterinarian (video)
children.text: Laboratory animal medicine and research

notes: Resources: Veterinary Medicine Teacher Overview (website)
Veterinarian for Working Dogs - Government (video)
children.text: Teaching and government

requirements.text: Discuss with your counselor the roles a veterinarian plays in the following:

notes: Resources: How Long Does It Take to Become a Veterinarian and Board Certified? (video)

requirements.text: Wildfire Suppression Tools. Do the following:

children.text: Develop a fire readiness plan for a wildland area with which you are familiar. The plan should include a map showing available resources, water supplies, natural and manmade barriers, and access. The plan should discuss fuel loads, available fire apparatus, structure protection needs, values at risk, medical and evacuation considerations and potential fire suppression tactics.

Visit with a state or federal forestry official or your local fire warden. Discuss the causes of and types of wildland fire that occur in your area. Discuss the prime fire season(s) in your area. Identify the agency responsible for wildland fire suppression in your area. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

children.text: Conduct a Firewise assessment of a home or a building in the wildland-urban interface, which could include a Scout camp building or facility. Identify potential risks and fire hazards. With your counselor's approval, complete a project to reduce the wildfire risk and increase the preparedness of the building. Write a brief report about what you did and learned from the assessment and project.

Meet with a Fire Prevention Specialist or a local fire official to learn about fire prevention efforts in your community. From what you learned, prepare a fire prevention message (skit, video, or billboard concept) and share with your counselor and troop (or other group approved by your counselor).

Meet with a meteorologist or someone familiar with fire weather and discuss the fire weather concerns and typical fire seasons that exist in your area. Discuss the conditions that lead to a Fire Weather Watch or a Red Flag Warning. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.
